attempts.label: DANDI:000941
attempts.paper_title: Spatiotemporal distribution of location and object effects in reach-to-grasp kinematics
attempts.entry_title: Location and object effects in reach-to-grasp kinematics (Rouse and Schieber 2015)
attempts.summary: None of the paper's main findings could be tested in this data. The findings that location effects dominate the shoulder and wrist and object effects the digits, that both emerge early in the reach, and that object effects grow to dominate before contact all rest on joint angles from motion capture, and the dataset holds no kinematics, only EMG and spikes. It also holds only one of the three monkeys and part of one session. The movement time could not be checked either, since the dataset's undefined onset time is very likely a later event than the paper's onset.
attempts.description: Tests the claims of Rouse and Schieber (2015) on dandiset 000941, the FALCON M1-A benchmark, which holds trial tables, EMG and multiunit spikes of monkey L, including part of the paper's session L20120928, and no marker positions or joint angles. It checks the trial counts and the movement time of the session, shows that the dataset's movement onset is a later event than the paper's, names the object codes from the paper's apparatus order, and records the kinematic claims as blocked.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Rouse and Schieber (2015) from dandiset 000941

outcomes.statement: In the three sessions the monkeys performed 768, 824 and 745 trials (L, X, Y), of which 717, 788 and 688 were successful and 685, 752 and 637 were analyzed.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Table 2
outcomes.quote: during these sessions the monkeys performed from 745 to 824 total trials, of which from 688 to 798 were performed successfully, with from 637 to 752 trials being retained for analysis
outcomes.notes: The file of session L20120928 (held-in-calib) holds 412 trials, all rewarded, numbered 201 to 673 (one stored as 127) and spanning 53.3 of the session's 86.2 minutes; the paper gives 768 trials, 717 successful and 685 analyzed. The file holds no failed trials, so neither the total nor the analyzed count can be formed, and it holds a part of the successful ones, the part released as the FALCON calibration split. If every number absent inside 201 to 673 were an error trial, the span would hold 473 trials, 412 successful and 387 with the preceding number present; this is not a count of the session. Monkeys X and Y are not in the dandiset.
deviations: Only the held-in-calib file of the session is counted; the minival file repeats its first two trials.

outcomes.statement: The median duration from movement onset to contact differs among the monkeys (255, 235 and 335 ms for L, X and Y; Kruskal-Wallis P < 0.001), giving 52, 48 and 68 normalized samples from M to C.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Table 2
outcomes.quote: The duration of the epoch from movement onset to peripheral object contact, which we refer to as the reach-to-grasp epoch, differed among the three monkeys ... with medians ranging from 235 to 335 ms

statistics.n: analyzed trials of three monkeys, one session each

outcomes.notes: Monkey L only. Taken at face value, the median of contact_time minus move_onset_time over the 412 successful trials of session L20120928 in the file is 200 ms (quartiles 160 and 240 ms), against 255 ms (225, 295) with tolerance 229.5 to 280.5 ms, 41 samples from M to C against 52; the approximation of the analyzed trials (preceding trial number present, 387 trials) gives the same 200 ms. The dandiset does not define move_onset_time, and the notebook indicates it is very likely not the paper's onset M. In all four monkey L sessions of the dandiset the file's median movement time (180, 200, 180, 200 ms) is 52 to 58 ms shorter than the authors' own median for the same session in Rouse and Schieber 2016, J Neurophysiol 115, Table 2 (238, 255, 232, 253 ms), three times the 20 ms step of the event times. The file's median cue to onset is 300 to 320 ms, 57 to 77 ms longer than the shortest session median of I-M that Rouse and Schieber 2016, J Neurosci 36, gives for monkey L (243 ms), while its median cue to contact (500 to 520 ms) is 4 to 25 ms above 243 ms plus the session's published movement time. Cue and contact agree with the papers and the onset comes about 55 ms after the paper's M, as a later event such as the task software's center-release event marker (2015 Methods, Behavioral Task) would. EMG aligned on the dataset's onset fits this (DLTa, BCPs and TCPlat reach half their peak 40 ms before it, 8 of 16 muscles reach half their peak before it), though EMG leads motion under any definition of onset. A movement time from a later event cannot test the paper's, and the paper's onset cannot be recomputed without markers. Monkeys X and Y are not in the dandiset (data_missing), so their medians, the difference among monkeys and the Kruskal-Wallis test cannot be tested either.
deviations: The dataset's move_onset_time and contact_time are used, as the claims file directs when the dataset gives onset times; the paper's onset (average speed of 36 markers above 5 SD of a baseline, Methods, Temporal Normalization) cannot be recomputed without markers. The notebook indicates the dataset's onset is very likely a later event, so the result is shown but not compared.

The dataset's onset is checked against reference values from two later papers of the same authors on the same monkey and sessions, in paper/ (J Neurophysiol 115:3238, Table 2, median movement time per session; J Neurosci 36:10640, Methods, which gives 243 ms as the minimum over monkey L's sessions of the median time from instruction to movement onset). They are used only to check the event, not to judge the claim.
Event times are at 20 ms resolution, where the paper's onset is at 5 ms and contact at 1 ms.

Only 412 of the session's 717 successful trials are in the dandiset; reading (a), the analyzed trials, is approximated by the trials whose preceding trial number is present, as the error trials are absent. Many absent numbers are more likely successful trials held back in FALCON splits not on DANDI, so this drops more trials than the paper's rule would; both readings give 200 ms.
Monkey L only; X and Y are not in the dandiset.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds no kinematic data. The paper's findings are about 22 joint angles computed from 36 markers tracked at 200 frames/s, and no file holds a marker position, a joint angle or any other kinematic series; the files hold trial tables, 16 channels of EMG at 50 Hz, an evaluation mask and multiunit spike times. 23 of the 26 claims are blocked for this reason.

Only monkey L is in the dandiset. The paper's monkeys X (session X20121219) and Y (Y20130516) are not; the description points to dandiset 001209 for another monkey, monkey X, as a draft with no published version; the claims file does not name it, so it is not used.

The paper's session L20120928 is in the dandiset only in part. Its held-in-calib file holds 412 trials, all rewarded, numbered 201 to 673 and spanning 53 of the session's 86 minutes, where the paper reports 768 trials and 717 successes. Within 201 to 673, 61 numbers are absent in gaps of 1 to 15; the files do not say which trials were left out, or why (errors, or trials held back for the benchmark's evaluation). The result column, described as success, failure or abort, holds R in every trial of every file.

tgt_obj, described as the object to grasp at the target, does not name the grasped object. In session 20120928 it takes three values (Sphere, Button, Coaxial) in three runs of 118, 159 and 135 consecutive trials, each value occurring with all four obj_id codes and every location. obj_id has four codes whose locations within each block are offset by multiples of 45 degrees, as the paper's apparatus has them, and the grasped object is decoded from EMG around contact at 0.99 with obj_id against 0.42 with tgt_obj (largest class 0.39).

obj_id, the actual object code, has no names. From the paper's Fig. 1 legend (clockwise order perpendicular cylinder, coaxial cylinder, button, sphere, with 157.5 degrees leftmost) and the locations at which each code occurs, codes 2, 1, 4 and 3 are the perpendicular cylinder, coaxial cylinder, button and sphere; the names fit every constraint the legend states, but the files do not confirm them.

In each of the four held-in-calib files one trial carries the number 127 between trials 254 and 256 or 257, in time order, where 255 (or 256) is expected; 127 is the largest signed 8-bit integer. In session 20120927 a second trial, the first of the file, is also numbered 127, so the number does not identify a trial there.

The event times move_onset_time, contact_time and reward_time are not defined, and all event times lie on a 20 ms grid. move_onset_time is very likely not the paper's movement onset. In each of the four monkey L sessions of the dandiset the median time from move_onset_time to contact_time (180 to 200 ms) is 52 to 58 ms shorter than the authors' own median for the session (238 to 255 ms, Rouse and Schieber 2016, J Neurophysiol 115, Table 2; 255 ms for 20120928 in the 2015 paper), and the median cue to onset (300 to 320 ms) is longer than the shortest median the authors give for monkey L (243 ms, J Neurosci 2016), while cue to contact agrees; the onset is about 55 ms later than the marker-speed onset, as the task software's center-release event marker would be. reward_time follows contact by a median of 0.10 s (0 to 0.92 s), where the paper's task requires a 1,000 ms hold before the reward. start_time and stop_time are exactly 1 s before the cue and 1 s after reward_time in every trial, a window, not the trial's start and stop.

Each held-in-minival file repeats the first two trials of the held-in-calib file of the same session (same trial numbers, event times, EMG timestamps and spike times on all 64 channels), as the description says. The EMG values of the two copies differ by a near-constant factor per file (0.955 to 1.016), so each file's EMG was scaled on its own, and the same recording has two different EMG amplitudes in the dandiset.

disagreements.reason: Blocked, metadata_insufficient for L and data_missing for X and Y. The notebook assumes move_onset_time is the paper's marker-speed onset M and never checks it. The EMG paper (jn.00008.2016) Table 2 gives medians of 238, 255, 232 and 253 ms for the same four sessions where the files give 180, 200, 180 and 200 ms, a steady shortfall of about 40 to 55 ms that a 20 ms grid cannot explain, and the files' median cue to onset of 300 ms exceeds the J Neurosci 2016 minimum median I-M of 243 ms. Together these point to a later onset event in the dataset, such as release of the center object, so not reproduced is not a sound reading. The verifier asked for the per-session medians next to that Table 2, cue to onset next to the I-M value, and mean EMG aligned on move_onset_time. It also noted floating-point residue in the printed per-session medians (cosmetic).

entries.name: rouse-2015
entries.title: Location and object effects in reach-to-grasp kinematics (Rouse and Schieber 2015)
entries.description: Tests the claims of Rouse and Schieber (2015) on dandiset 000941, the FALCON M1-A benchmark, which holds trial tables, EMG and multiunit spikes of monkey L, including part of the paper's session L20120928, and no marker positions or joint angles. It checks the trial counts and the movement time of the session, shows that the dataset's movement onset is a later event than the paper's, names the object codes from the paper's apparatus order, and records the kinematic claims as blocked.
